question: Should we bear each other's burdens?
summary: Galatians 6:2 commands believers to bear one another's burdens. Three verses later, Galatians 6:5 says every person shall bear his own burden. The same paragraph from the same author gives diametrically opposite directives about whose burden you carry.

reconcile.connective: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown read the two verses as complementary, not contradictory, since Paul uses a different Greek word for "burden" in each.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells's Skeptic's Annotated Bible lists the two verses as a flat Yes/No contradiction to the question "Should we bear each other's burdens?"

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, Skeptic's Annotated Bible (1999), contra/burden.html

pd_work.resource: John Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John Haley
pd_work.note: Haley treats this exact pair under the heading 'Burdens' (parallel columns 'Must bear others' burdens' / 'Bear our own burdens'), stating: 'The original word for "burden" is not the same in the two cases... The first text means, "Be sympathetic and helpful to each other in the midst of infirmities and sorrows"; the second, "Every man must bear his own responsibility, under the Divine government."'

excerpts.excerpt_text: This verse does not contradict Gal 6:2. There he tells them to bear with others' "burdens" of infirmity in sympathy; here, that self-examination will make a man to feel he has enough to do with "his own load" of sin, without comparing himself boastfully with his neighbor.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly denies the contradiction between 6:2 and 6:5 and explains the different senses ('burdens' of infirmity borne in sympathy vs. one's own 'load' of sin) behind the two occurrences of 'burden.'
excerpts.source_note_text: For (by this way, Gal 6:4, of proving himself, not depreciating his neighbor by comparison) each man shall bear his own "burden," or rather, "load" (namely, of sin and infirmity), the Greek being different from that in Gal 6:2. This verse does not contradict Gal 6:2. There he tells them to bear with others' "burdens" of infirmity in sympathy; here, that self-examination will make a man to feel he has enough to do with "his own load" of sin, without comparing himself boastfully with his neighbor. Compare Gal 6:3. Instead of "thinking himself to be something," he shall feel the "load" of his own sin: and this will lead him to bear sympathetically with his neighbor's burden of infirmity.
